In various fields including statistical physics, machine learning, and combinatorics, a prevalent challenge involves identifying local minimizers of non-concave functions defined on high-dimensional spaces. Addressing this, we introduce and formulate the Theory-Assisted Message Passing (post-AMP) algorithm, an advancement over standard AMP that integrates a novel message passing mechanism initialized with AMP's output. This initiative combines the efficiency of empirical methods with the reliability of theoretical insights: data-driven assumptions narrow down the complex landscape of possibilities, while rigorous mathematics validates the superiority of the resulting solutions. We demonstrate this synergy through a concrete message passing kernel within a communications channel corrupted by additive Gaussian noise; our derived algorithm is proven to converge to a local minimum of the entropy function for observed samples. Furthermore, we present a rigorous proof that the "TAP free energy" is locally convex relative to its optimal arguments—a key mathematical result essential for ensuring the convergence of descent algorithms starting from AMP's initial values.

During disruptions, privately owned electric vehicles (POEVs) can serve as a mobile reserve of energy strength by sharing grid power and enabling deliveries, thereby boosting resilience. However, the potential of this resource often remains suboptimal due to individual driver priorities and limited visibility into private data. To address this and enhance the grid's ability to recover and operate during failures, we developed a multi-agent optimization (MAO) model. This framework evaluates pull factors—such as price and distance—used by drivers when selecting superchargers, simultaneously optimizing for factors like travel, charging, and shipping costs. Our model maximizes total system utility while minimizing logistics and charging expenses through 1) the estimation of supercharger demand using a random utility model (RAM) and 2) the formulation of a mixed-integer linear program (MILP). We validate our approach by demonstrating how MAO informs strategic investments in supercharger infrastructure and logistics using data from a real-world case in California. Additionally, simulations indicate that MIS information-driven POEV movements during outages could enable up to 27% more transferable energy and 95% more completed trips than optimized scenarios. Finally, comparing different resilience strategies shows that utilizing POEV capacity for moving goods yields higher total system utility than using it solely for charging.

Applications of the proposed algorithm extend to collaborative navigation to intersections, communication contact maintenance via scheduled appointments, and distributed computation through scheduled interactions.

Silicon and doped silicon serve as the primary electrical platforms globally, with research increasingly focused on developing tandem architectures to integrate optical and digital circuits. A critical objective in creating a robust all-light-based system is advancing light interconnects capable of reaching both short and long distances while maintaining high bandwidth and power efficiency. Although silicon supports efficient routers based on ring resonators and $\lambda/8$ bends, current technologies lack a corresponding robust platform for straight propagators—often identified as T junction (T hubs)—despite these components being fundamental for interconnect routing systems. Surprisingly, testing reveals that T hubs fabricated in silicon exhibit exceptional performance when paired with high-index light-guiding rods. These structures function as compact, resonant filters exhibiting insertion losses below $-3.5\text{ dB}$ and crosstalk under $-20\text{ dB}$. Additionally, these devices demonstrate scalable manufacturing and process resilience against variations in manufacturing dimensions and residual stress. However, performance metrics degrade significantly when using lower thickness dimensions or poly-silicon materials. We attribute the superior outcomes with single-crine thin films to minimized stress-induced index changes and precise control over feature geometry. Consequently, these optimized T hubs provide a promising building block for comprehensive on-chip photointelectrical hub systems.

This paper investigates whether word embeddings capture the emotional tone measured by the Loughran-McDonald (LC) sentiment analyzer. While prior research has largely relied on validating these representations through various tests, we argue that assessing their face validity—specifically in the context of financial text—is essential. Consequently, we apply the widely respected LC algorithm to our primary evaluation. Our analysis reveals a significant negative correlation between absolute value and embedding magnitude, indicating that doesopic intensity in representations fails to mirror sentiment strength. Furthermore, visual inspections of radial plots and scalarings fail to faithfully reproduce the LC spectrum, and embeddings cannot correctly classify LC-text's polarities. By addressing an applied concern often overlooked, this work offers a critical perspective on sentiment-specific vocabulary.

This work proposes novel configurations using different transmitter architectures to match the performance of the "Broadband Waveforming for Integrated Data and Power Delivery" scheme, specifically replacing either a Single-Tone configuration, a Multi-Tone setup, or a Single-Antna Multi-Carrier (SAMC) single configuration. This paper introduces a novel numerical approach for solving three-dimensional solidification and melting problems by integrating a level-set method with an embedded boundary technique. This combination allows the differential equations governing the thermal process to be solved separately in the solid and liquid regions. While this decoupled strategy is simple, it introduces numerical difficulties near the solid-liquid interface, particularly when resolving the steep temperature gradients in the liquid zone. The embedded boundary method addresses these challenges and has been validated against two exact analytical solutions and a established finite element code. These validations demonstrate that the proposed scheme is an effective and precise tool for simulating coupled solidification and melting phenomena.

Adapting particle distribution functions (PDFs) to account for new or varied experimental data has become increasingly significant. This adaptation underlies nearly all modern experimental analyses and plays a vital role in many theoretical frameworks. Although various adjustment methods exist, they typically lack rigorous justification, creating the risk of misleading outcomes. In contrast, this study proposes an adjustment methodology grounded in Bayesian inference. While not the first application of Bayesian principles to this context, our approach explicitly incorporates prior knowledge regarding parameter uncertainties associated with theoretical model components. We demonstrate through a case study involving single inclusive cross-sections that neglecting these uncertainty terms can compromise both the reliability of results and the efficiency of parameter estimation.

Supportive experiments conducted across various standard RL benchmarks validate our approach, confirming its superiority over other strategies employing different weighting preferences.

We introduce a dialogue branching system designed to significantly expand the total number of feasible conversation paths. We illustrate our approach, named MTDog, and demonstrate its efficacy on both public and three private datasets. The method employs an efficient and adaptable framework utilizing an enhanced decoder that generates multiple child responses for any given dialogue history. This process continues iteratively until reaching a predetermined depth, effectively creating a highly branched dialogue structure capable of engaging in diverse dialogues from any given initial user input. We evaluate the demonstrated capability of this generated dialogue structure from multiple angles, supporting our findings with visualizations and quantitative metrics taken from both public and private datasets. Additionally, we assess the system's efficiency and manageability through experimental framework analysis, concluding that this proposal offers a straightforward solution for diverse dialogue generation that can be easily integrated and expanded upon existing architectures.

The Telescoper and Urban air shower detectors are advanced LHC instrumentation designed to analyze rare, dense environments characterized by low multiplicity and high occupancy. These include proton-lead (pPb), light ion collisions (such as p-P, p-P-P, and p-P-P-P), and low-multiplicity proton-proton (pp) events. Transient X-ray binaries located in the Galactic Centre region are suspected to possess repetition intervals ($T_{\rm rep}$) shorter than one year, yet these intervals remain poorly constrained due to the high concentration of sources and observational difficulties associated with continuous, long-duration monitoring. Leveraging superior access to the Galactic Centre provided by the KATRIN instrument at the 8-m Keck Telescope, we conducted observations of four specific transients—XMM CYSOG, HMCYSOG, GTCMYSOC, and GTCMYSOG—over multiple seasons to accurately determine their $T_{\rm rep}$. The findings revealed $T_{\rm rep}$ values of $0.6\pm0.1$, $<0.4$, $<0.38$, and $<0.34$ respectively for the four targets. We synthesized these new limits with prior constraints from various telescopes to infer properties of the Galactic Centre's dormant X-ray transient population. While a strong correlation between $T_{\rm rep}$ and transient severity exists, it likely arises from a selection effect rather than an intrinsic physical mechanism. Furthermore, because the most luminous events were not captured within our study, current limits on $T_{\rm rep}$ likely underestimate the true values found in the area.

This study explores various strategies for integrating different types of experimental data, including threshold, resonance shape, and cross section measurements, into amplitude analysis. A key distinction is drawn between phase and amplitude data; phase information tends to be well-constrained by standard analyses, making additional shape or shape data less critical. In contrast, amplitude information is inherently noisier and benefits significantly from external constraints. We argue that the inclusive incorporation of all data types is best achieved not merely through arbitrary methods, but by applying appropriate likelihood constructions for each specific context.

Establishing a fundamental framework for classifying and analyzing the diverse physical processes behind gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) and their afterglows remains an elusive objective. In response, we introduce a new, cohesive dynamical progression that unifies the diverse afterglow phenomena observed following long-duration Burat 0910+09 (an X-ray flash) within a single descriptive structure. This model builds upon our previously established Higher-Order Radiation (HOR) framework, which was designed to describe the progressive dynamics seen in afterglows. The result is a novel, general progression of events that successfully accounts for both the varied radiative behaviors of these bursts and their corresponding light curves.

During this evolution, a burst transitions through sequential dynamial stages: it moves from an regime dominated by radiative friction in the relativistic domain to one dominated by radiative effects during sub-relativistic motion. The progression continues, eventually reaching a phase where internal shocks dominate in the non-relativistic regime. This final stage produces afterglow emissions and stellar-like radiative decay in both UV and optical bands. The identified dynamics provide a comprehensive explanation for the observed R-band light curves, spectral energy distributions (SED), and radiative decay patterns of Burat 0910+09, while the final non-relativistic internal shock stage specifically accounts for the R-component often referred to as the "internal jet."

Vertical federated learning (FEDLEARN) represents a promising approach to enhancing intelligence across multiple domains while keeping data localized, thereby addressing many privacy concerns. However, this method potentially exposes participants to other significant privacy risks. In this paper, we investigate the link between vertical federated learning and privacy attacks, introducing a specific threat known as "pragmatic privacy attacks." Unlike similar concepts, these attacks prioritize both high utility for the attacking party and strong guarantees of individual privacy. To achieve this balance, we formulate the challenge as a stochastic mixed-integer programming problem. Within this model, we define and incorporate key dimensions such as the target attribute for inference, acceptable privacy levels, required utility, and constraints related to mutual confidentiality in federated settings. Our proposed framework demonstrates through comprehensive simulations that effective pragmatic privacy attacks are feasible; furthermore, we show that a solution derived via our proposed stochastic mixed-integer programming offers a superior trade-off between privacy and utility compared to both pure pragmatic privacy attacks and standard federated learning practices.

In this work, we introduce a novel approach for computing the empirical kernel matrix, which is a crucial and frequently utilized structure in many algorithms within the domain of high-dimensional and large-scale machine learning. Our method leverages Pseudo Random Fourier (PRF) point evaluations to produce a dense kernel matrix, enabling data-dependent kernel estimation that presents a meaningful trade-off between computational efficiency and performance. To address diverse classification challenges, we formulate an optimized matrix construction strategy. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposal when applied in this practical context.

This paper investigates the optimal allocation of resources in wireless systems that support both wireless information transmission (WIT) and energy harvesting (WEH). Our goal is to determine how to distribute transmit power spectrum and allocation to simultaneously maximize information transmission rate and harvested energy. In this context, we consider a scenario where an information transmitter (IT) sends data to multiple co-channel recipients, drawing its power from a transmitter with in-remote (RIT). The proposed model accounts for non-linear energy conversion at each node, which changes the efficiency of energy harvesting based on received signal power levels. To address this problem, we formulate an optimization model that seeks to find the optimal allocation of transmit power and bandwidth for an IT node to achieve the highest total data rate and energy harvest within the network constraints. Since this problem, which includes non-linear energy conversion and multiple services, cannot be easily solved, we derive a closed-form initial solution that provides the best starting point. Various numerical examples are presented to demonstrate the validity of the proposed method and explore how different parameters affect the optimal allocation.

A standard technique in statistical mechanics involves analyzing standard models through non-linear equation systems known as mean-field theories. Although these systems typically require proof to ensure the uniqueness of their solutions, demonstrating such proofs can be difficult. We focus on the epidemic contact process defined on a Cayley graph within an arbitrary nilpotent group, showing that a unique solution indeed emerges from our mean-field framework. The significance of nilpotent groups extends beyond group theory; nilpotency serves as a key geometric characteristic indicating flatness at large scales, which is equivalent to the "avalanche scale" in our context. Because of this equivalence, mastering the epidemic contact process on Cayley graphs in nilpotent groups functions as a representative "minimal nilpotent model" for understanding similar processes on structures with avalanche-scale geometries.

This study details the adaptation of a Sloshing-Sagnac interferometer for use as strain sensor within a gravitational wave (GW) detector. Building upon existing designs, it presents enhanced strategies for strain measurement utilizing the Sagnac loop present in the main interferometer. Analysis of both numerical simulations and physical experiments validates that this configuration achieves superior short-strain resolution compared to conventional methods. Specifically, it demonstrates a tenfold enhancement in resolution for frequencies exceeding 100 Hz, without compromising performance at lower frequencies or static measurements. Consequently, detectors are able to detect vertex sloshing disturbances arising from GW-detectored seismic noise, which can significantly aid source localization and mitigate confusion caused by spurious signals.

This paper introduces a Media Access Control (MAC) control protocol designed for XL-MIMO systems that employ a point-to-point communication model within an environment featuring a random, static visibility partition. However, an important finding reveals that if the estimated visibility area is confirmed to be truly non-intersected, it is mathematically impossible to determine the exact boundaries between these disjoint regions using only observable data. This result holds regardless of whether the observer knows the underlying random process used for generation or possesses complete statistical insights about it.

Despite this limitation, the authors demonstrate that sufficient information can still be gathered to design an efficient, practical algorithm. This algorithm achieves logarithmic complexity with respect to the number of radiation sectors while only requiring coarse information about the probabilistic nature of the visibility partition at the receiver.

Although neural networks have largely superseded traditional linguistic models due to their superior fluency in drafting neural stories, this study questions whether that shift was entirely necessary. To address this, we propose a language generation task framework that introduces learned crime solution histories, enabling the integration of complete exact-match $n$-gram features. Furthermore, although our method stands out for restoring complete input data, it applies equally when other constraints result in reduced information from traditional models. Our experiments utilizing extended text generation task demonstrate that the suggested method dramatically boosts output quality compared to baseline systems that abandon existing patterns, confirming that collaboration between neural and traditional techniques outperforms approaches where they compete.

Achiezing accurate 3D face alignment and reconstruction in uncontrolled environments remains a difficult task due to disturbances caused by poor lighting, occlusions, and varying poses. Most current solutions address 2D facial alignment first, generating a initial 3D model via forward or inverse rendering, which then uses regularisation to enforce consistency with the image; however, this paper argues that such an indirectly 3D-driven workflow, relying on regularisation forces, is prone to errors and limits overall performance. Building upon a 2D dual-network alignment system, we introduce "Self-aligned Dual Facial Regression Networks" (SDFRNet), which diverges by performing 1-to-1 and N-to-1 facial mapping separately to deliver robust 2D results. Consequently, we generate a rough, unregularised 3D model for two distinct phase: one dedicated to dense facial reconstruction and the other toReverence. Key innovations include a new cross-domain self-attention mechanism that enables cross-domain point correspondence between 2D and 3D data, as well as a boundary-aware self-adaptive mechanism designed to handle difficult edges. Extensive tests across multiple public benchmarks show that SARDFNet outperforms the latest state-of-the-art methods in both 2D facial alignment and 3D reconstruction.

In the increasingly complex and expansive electric markets, the strategic deployment of Machine Learning (ML) and AI by generators, consumers, and retailers holds significant promise. This research explores end-to-end cross-domain text-to-SQL tasks, addressing limitations of existing models that achieve high accuracy on benchmark datasets yet produce poorly parsed SQL statements unsuitable for database execution. To mitigate this issue, we introduce a differential item functioning (DIE) -based SQL statement parser alongside a tailored classification problem, thereby creating two sub-stages from the domain challenge. This study demonstrates that imposing Lipschitz constraints on neural network architectures can be achieved by applying a suitable variance reduction type of gradient check. Specifically, we introduce a novel algorithm, DLCX, capable of training a model with enforced Lipschitz continuity. DLCX requires only a single pass over the dataset per parameter update and converges efficiently to form a suitable approximation of the original loss function with bounded Lipschitz constant $K = \mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{t})$, where $t$ represents training epochs. Using this approach, we successfully trained a defensive model to protect against $l_\infty$-bounded adversarial examples with both PNG and CIFAR inputs, achieving a lower Lipschitz constant and exhibiting superior defensive capabilities compared to a neural network trained with the standard DLC method.

Centering theory has long been recognized as a robust method for understanding local coreferential patterns. This investigation aims to integrate the theory into a mainstream neural coreference solver by employing it to refine the predictions of a pre-processing step. Our analysis involves augmenting raw text with features derived from Centering Theory, using these enhanced texts to train a neural coreferential classifier. Subsequently, these predictions are used to re-verifiable resolve anaphora within a coreferential solving system based on Rule plus Neural Networks. WiFi signal strength, measured in decibel milliwatts (dBm), offers a way to estimate range, though this correlation is often ambiguous due to environmental variables. This work introduces a supervised machine learning approach using K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) to improve estimation accuracy. The proposed model was tested within an office building using 1000 capture samples across 30 access points to generate training and testing datasets. An optimized assessment strategy involving a filtered subset of the training data was developed; rather than utilizing all 1000 instances, only the most representative points were selected to create a streamlined system. The method described here represents the initial application of the KNN algorithm to raw, real-world WiFi data.

Beam fragmentation instability represents a fundamental physical challenge in energy recovery linacs (ERLs), critically limiting the achievable luminosity for atomic physics applications. Within this context, enhancing the lifetime of circulating beam particles before instability causes loss is essential for sustaining high instantaneous luminosity. Recent research by the SLCCRL ERL team demonstrated that an optimal life time can be achieved by carefully selecting the vertical fill pattern; consequently, their study focused on methods to manipulate this initial vertical distribution. To do so, they conducted experiments within their ERL facility using various apertured drift sections positioned between the energy recovery cavity and the diagonal crossing point at the light collection station. Their findings revealed a strong dependence of particle life time relative to the aperture and total distance traveled. Ultimately, the research team established that luminosity levels sufficient for atomic scale investigations are attainable by optimizing the initial electron configuration.

This derivation via field theoret methods compleons to a previous finding obtained via world-sheet representations in string theory and holds a practical significance for precise phenomenological studies of proton-proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC).

When a molened polymer brush is subjected to sufficiently intense lateral forces, the strong shear induces flow that erodes the brush layer, forcing chains to reorganize and the system to reach a new steady elongated balance. This phenomenon, known as end exclusion, has previously been modeled only for surfaces elongated in one direction, analyzed via a mean-field approach that neglected hydrodynamic interactions and relied on a force-minimization framework to determine the new brush parameters. This study extends that methodology to surfaces of complex, strongly elongated shapes by incorporating a novel, rigorous derivation of capillary tension alongside our assumed lateral force. Findings from this general framework reveal two primary outcomes: first, the magnitude of capillary tension dictates whether chains migrate laterally or the original contact point simply shifts; second, perturbations arising from local brush features—such as variations in spacing—can accumulate capillary tension to a degree that completely displaces chains from those regions. Consequently, for any specific lateral force and capillary tension pair acting on a surface of intricate elongated geometry, there exists a capillary scale range where the effect fails to be "strong," meaning no exclusion zones emerge.

For any finite connected graph $\G = (V, E)$, its \textit{metric dimension} is defined as the minimum possible size of a \textit{resolving set}. A set $W \subseteq V$ qualifies as resolving set when, for every pair of distinct vertices $u$ and $v$ in $G$, there exists at least one $w \in W$ such that the distance $d(u,w)$ differs from $d(v,w)$; in other words, vertices in such a set are uniquely identified by their distance vectors relative to $W$. Recognizing that the metric dimension holds applications in diverse fields, this study aims to establish both upper and lower bounds for this parameter. We also investigate specific graph families, offering results on matchable graphs, graphs possessing a perfect matching, matchable trees, and more generally, rooted trees. Furthermore, we define and explore a related invariant known as \textit{shortened metric dimension}. Our analysis determines the exact values for this new invariant across several of the previously mentioned graph classes and compares it directly to the standard metric dimension. Distinctive features of the paper include a closed-form calculation for the shortened metric dimension of matchable graphs and the derivation of multiple characterizations for resolving sets within rooted trees.

Thus, the model provides a probabilistic outlook for each target, helping future surveys concentrate on regions most likely to yield novel discoveries. We further categorize the samples into sub-classes, such as flat-spectrum quasars, radio-quiet blazars, and non-blazar interstellar medium, which could guide where to look for specific types of objects.

The study further proposes the validity test for this principle on various proteins, categorizing them based on their adherence: highly consistent proteins with natural knotting processes may allow inferences regarding their biogenesis mechanisms.

In this work, we address the problem of linear regression with categorical variables and propose a new method called EMC-Group Lasso. Traditional Group Lasso, an prevalent technique for this domain, often under-performs because of its poor scalability and inability to identify optimal dummy variable subsets effectively. Extensive numerical simulations and analysis of a large-scale real-world dataset demonstrate that EMC-Group Lasso not only estimates parameters with superior accuracy but also provides a more robust and interpretable model for real applications, surpassing the results obtained from standard Group Lasso.

In this paper, we introduce Decision-based Transferable White-box Support (DTWS), a novel decision-based framework designed to accelerate knowledge acquisition from decision-black-box classifiers for new, unrelated datasets. This method enables the extraction of significant information from a seemingly random model with the same architecture, allowing it to be applied across multiple cases without requiring retraining. By utilizing a single transferable white-box model, DTWS employs two distinct approaches to probe decision-black-box classifiers: first, it generates a targeted perturbation that maximally alters their output, and second, it derives a local surrogate to approximate their underlying logic. Together, these strategies serve to bridge the gap in current transferable attacks, which typically focus on only one type of probe. Extensive experiments conducted on six datasets using various black-listed architectures demonstrate that DTWS effectively utilizes decryptions to validate the robustness of white-list solutions. Additionally, this study examines the duration of successful attacks and provides a detailed comparison of known transferable methods.

Asynchronous Federated Training (AFT) has emerged as a primary strategy to accelerate federated learning by reducing training iterations through concurrent model updates from multiple rounds. Our research indicates, however, that while increasing frequency of these updates linearly increases training throughput, it concurrently decreases accuracy; specifically, gradient unconstrainedness—the lack of regulation for updates from highly active clients—acts as the root cause of this performance decline. We demonstrate that even a single unconstrained update can nullify the improvements gained by asynchronous training. Consequently, we propose asynchronous federated training with buffered synchronous aggregation (SFT), which selectively discards excessive unconstrained updates to preserve accuracy while minimizing, rather than eliminating, update frequency. Surprisingly, even with frequent reliance on this buffered synchronous approach, the method achieves near-identical performance to state-of-the-art AFT using frozen validation, confirming that gradient unconstrainedness must be managed to ensure both high accuracy and efficient training.

Although advanced digital signal processing techniques effectively mitigate most errors in wireless systems, rare occurrences of uncorrectable failures can still lead to signal dropouts. To minimize this risk, we propose an innovative scheme that integrates physical layer security measures into multi-carrier (MC) frameworks. In our approach, specific subcarriers within the carrier system are intentionally allocated lower power levels to act as sacrificial elements. The resulting distribution of transmit power across all channels remains continuous and concave. This design ensures that if security breaches happen on the compromised low-power subcarriers, overall data stream integrity is preserved. We evaluate and compare the suggested method against two traditional security-tiered models—discrete and smooth power allocations—in terms of both computational requirements and bit error rate (BER) performance. Our findings indicate that the proposed continuous and concave allocation strategy imposes higher complexity than the discrete approach while demonstrating superior robustness compared to the smooth method.

This paper introduces the concept of grading collection polarization, a technique designed to enhance the descriptive capability of classical collections while maintaining efficient storage. We define P(P) as the polarization operator, which transforms a standard collection P into a structured graded collection. We investigate theoretical properties of our approach, offering a hierarchical generalization of both canonical sorting systems and conventional row-based filtering. Empirical assessments via large-scale human-centered experiments on three diverse domains—films, music, and coffee—demonstrate that our method effectively establishes an intuitive grading framework for each category. We also introduce and publish the inaugural "Coffee Datasets," comprising trained human graders who levelled extensive music and film datasets to create improved indexed datasets of corresponding graded collections. These findings establish Collection Polarization as a robust formalization for organizing information across varying complexities.

This study introduces a new mixed finite element method for discretizing Single-Phase Darcy flow across fractured, porous domains. The approach models fluid movement within both matrix blocks and fracture networks using a Spatial Hierarchy Continuous Element (SPACE) technique. Our formulation employs $C^0$-continuous finite elements on the fractured region $\Omega$ to approximate fracture permeability velocities, while simultaneously approximating the pressure field. Specifically, velocity is treated as a discontinuous quantity, partitioned into two components: $\v D$-continuous parts defined over the fractured domain $\Omega$ and node-connected values along fractures $\mathcal{T}$. This velocity formulation explicitly accounts for the friction coefficient (BEARING EDGE COEFFICIENT) at intersections between fractures and matrix blocks.

This method is notably simpler compared to existing hybrid finite models. Unlike those approaches, it does not require constructing a dual network by adding dual edges that cut through the domain to bridge fractures and matrix interfaces. We have also omitted the need to define specific interface flux variables. The theoretical foundations for the proposed method include proofs demonstrating the existence and uniqueness of the discrete solution. Finally, numerical experiments are presented to validate the method's efficacy and verify its computed convergence rates.

Illness-aware image modification involves transforming healthy images into ill ones that exhibit comparable structural changes between both groups, a technique with significant value for enhancing artificial intelligence (AA) for medical image analysis and developing novel diagnostic support systems. This study investigates the creation of synthetic pathological findings within normal chest X-rays and evaluates whether learned representations by recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are more effective than those by convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in categorizing these findings. Using a dataset of 1,000 de novo-generated pulmonary edema (PE) cases matched in distribution to 1,000 actual PE instances, we adjusted parameter settings within both CNN and CNN architectures to ensure uniform performance on the genuine PE dataset prior to adjustment. Results indicate that models trained on synthetic data achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.751 for PE detection, surpassing the 0.691 AUC achieved using only genuine PE data; accordingly, we conclude that synthetic integration yields superior single-site performance against real, matched distributions for this specific pathology, recognizing that while this outcome may not universally apply, it offers a promising avenue for enhancing model efficacy for PE detection. Additionally, our experimental framework provides essential protocols for future investigations utilizing synthetic augmentation, including optimal parameter strategies for model calibration with synthetic versus real pathology, and comparative assessments of direct versus combined training methodologies.
